chapter: Mellophone, Brunswick records and the West End Roof
title: The West End Roof manager who wanted Art Hickman music
summary: Hazel tells how he quit when a new manager demanded society music, and describes the 'you can't stump us' sign.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: Yeah. No it was the West End Roof. And that used to be a popular place out there. For all the college kids you know. So was. So was my place. That's the high. It was funny how I come to leave. Yeah. We'd been there for about two years. Two years and a half. So they changed managers. They got some guy from California. By the name of Johnson. Come in as manager you see. And at that time Art Hickman was the rage. In California you see. So he wanted me to play music like Art Hickman. So. All we used to get up there was like I tell you. The college kids. And it was a dollar to get in and two cents tax. But I always had to carry a pocket full of pennies. Because the guys would scramble up there. They'd get twenty cents from this guy. And dime from that guy. Until they got that buck. And they'd come up you see. And I'd have to always give them the two cents for the tax. But you got a thousand of them up there. Bill that was a thousand dollars. So we used to pack that place up there for seven nights a week. Those days. No no no off nights then you know. And we used to pack that place. But that man couldn't. If we got fifteen people out of the hotel. We got plenty. You see.

But he wanted me to play for the people in the hotel. I told him. I said. If I play for the people in the hotel. You ain't have nobody up there. So. We all get about it. Two three months you know. And finally I told him. I said. Look mister. Let me tell you one thing. I said. What you don't know about New Orleans will fill one book. And what you don't know about jazz will fill another book. I said. Now you want Art Hickman to get music up there. You get somebody else. Not me. I said. If I ever go there and play that way for them kids. They run me out of town. And if they would too. You come around with that chooky music with those kids. You know. They were born and raised on that music. And you had to play it for them. And we had to. Of course we didn't only play it. The boy at Dixieland now. The way they use it now. Bill had disgust me. Because we never. We played those tunes yeah. But that ain't all. We played. We played anything man. If a tune would come out of like the old swinging. The old spinning wheel you know.

We'd play the tune. But we'd play it our way. We'd play it in the New Orleans way. You know. And swing it. And so we used to have a sign on the piano. That you can't stump us. I had a regular sign up on the piano. Made out of some kind of glass. It was the first time I ever saw that. Like the sparkle. Oh yeah.

And I had that up on the piano. And we could play any way. If we didn't know the tune. We'd get you to hum it to us. You know. If we got the eight bars. That's all we needed was the first eight bars. Cause the channel would take care of itself. You know. Use number one. Number two. Number three. Middle. And. requests that we can't fill or something, you know, something like that. And it come up and we didn't know the tune, somebody in the band didn't know the tune, we'd say, well, hum it to us, you know. And then, all we needed was the first eight bars, the channel would take care of itself, you know, use number one, number two, number three, middle. And then, that's how I come to the leave up there. Now, where do we go from here?
